idiom_name: protocol plus struct fake injected through the initializer
implementation_notes: Injected protocols are the seam: the production type conforms to PriceServiceProtocol and a small struct in the test target conforms as well and returns canned data, so the compiler checks the stand-in against the protocol with no framework involved. Swift Testing supplies the harness - the @Test macro, #expect and #require, traits for per-test conditions - but deliberately ships no mocking facility, so the double is always hand-written, and that cost is low because protocol conformance plus a value type is a few lines. grpc-swift generates the production counterpart, a client type whose methods mirror the service and that the client calls exactly as it calls the fake.
pitfalls: A struct fake records calls into a copied value, so call-count assertions inside the double are lost; a recording double has to be a class or capture into an external reference.
An @MainActor-isolated protocol makes the fake actor-isolated too, so injecting it from a nonisolated context needs awaits or an explicit isolation hop, which is easy to misread as a production bug.
Protocol extensions supply default implementations, so a fake can silently inherit behaviour the real type overrides; check that the conformance implements the operations the test relies on.

variants.name: grpc-swift generated client (production seam)
variants.idiom_name: generated Client type from the .proto service definition
variants.implementation_notes: grpc-swift generates model and client code from the .proto file, producing a client type whose methods mirror the service and perform the remote call, so the same client code that ran against FakePrices runs against the generated client with a different dependency. Swift 5.x projects use gRPC Swift 1 (maintenance mode) and gRPC Swift 2 is the current major version, so the generated API shape depends on the generator version.
pitfalls: The generated client is a real client: tests still need a server, so either run an in-process service implementation or keep the protocol seam for unit tests.
Generated code is checked in or built by a plugin; a stale generated client compiles against an older contract without complaint.
